result: 18 severely affected post-COVID patients (61% meeting CCC ME/CFS) had lower peak power (1.1 vs 2.4 W/kg) and peak VO2 (16.0 vs 26.5 mL/min/kg) than 18 sex/age/BMI-matched healthy controls on a single symptom-limited CPET.
reason: Same measure (single-CPET peak VO2) in long COVID, same direction; small n, controls healthy rather than explicitly recovered, larger deficit fits severe selection.

result: Daily tracking of 10 PEM symptoms for 7 days before and 14 days after one maximal CPET in 18 severe PCC patients showed only a transient, clinically non-relevant increase lasting 1-3 days with no prolonged exacerbation, not differing by DSQ-PEM or ME/CFS status.
reason: Directly tests post-exertional symptom response in long COVID; adds a severe, PEM-screened sample with 14-day tracking showing transient (under 72 h) worsening, so it informs the contested finding rather than replicating one side.

result: In 6.1 million Swedish twins and siblings with register ICD diagnoses, heritability of functional somatic syndromes (including ME/CFS) and internalizing disorders was 15-44%, and ME/CFS had a modest genetic correlation with immune-mediated diseases (rA within 0.19-0.29).
reason: Twin-sibling heritability of register-diagnosed ME/CFS in a very large cohort extends family/twin evidence and adds a genetic correlation with immune-mediated disease; ME/CFS-specific h2 not stated in abstract.

result: 16S profiling of ME/CFS, long COVID and healthy controls found no alpha-diversity difference, small beta-diversity differences, and in both patient groups enrichment of Sutterella and depletion of Terrisporobacter and Lachnospiraceae.
reason: Lachnospiraceae depletion is consistent with butyrate-producer loss, but the paper does not report F. prausnitzii, named butyrate producers or butyrate capacity, so it is weak supporting evidence rather than a replication.

result: Direct comparison found overlapping but non-identical gut microbiome alterations in ME/CFS and long COVID versus controls (shared Sutterella up, Terrisporobacter and Lachnospiraceae down), with smaller differences between ME/CFS and LC than between either and controls.
reason: Supports the 'mirroring ME/CFS' part with a direct same-framework comparison, but does not test admission prediction or R. gnavus, so it extends rather than replicates.

result: Long COVID POTS patients, versus recovered non-POTS controls, had higher monocyte mitochondrial content and superoxide, lower NRF2 antioxidant enzymes, more monocyte isolevuglandins, 3-fold more circulating T cell-monocyte doublets with IFN-g/IL-17A-producing effector T cells correlating with severity, and raised IL-17A, IFN-g and TNF-a; tVNS reduced doublets, IsoLGs and monocyte IL-6 in a subset.
reason: Specific measured immune result (domain: immune, long COVID POTS) not covered; immune-longcovid-overlap only mentions myeloid shifts and exhausted T cells broadly.

result: In 19 hospital employees with post-COVID syndrome (7 meeting ME/CFS criteria) vs 23 controls, grip strength tended to be lower at some points without a consistent group effect, and fell in the second session 60 min later in patients but not controls.
reason: Same repeated-grip protocol with 60-min recovery, but in post-COVID with mixed results (no consistent strength deficit, poorer recovery), so a long COVID extension rather than a clean replication.

result: In NHIS 2021-2023 (86,655 US adults), an estimated 1.5% had ever received an ME/CFS diagnosis, of whom 20.7% reported no longer having it.
reason: Same NHIS self-reported diagnosis measure as Vahratian 2023 with an extra year, adding ever-diagnosed prevalence and a current/past split; overlapping data so not an independent replication.

result: Of US adults ever diagnosed with ME/CFS, 20.7% reported no longer having it, but 40-50% of these had symptoms and function similar to current cases and only about 25% were substantially better, and the past group stayed impaired versus never-diagnosed adults.
reason: Population-level self-report data consistent with low true recovery (roughly 5% of ever-diagnosed substantially improved), adding a national-survey perspective to cohort recovery rates.

result: Systematic review of 47 studies (over 25,000 long COVID patients) estimated pooled prevalence of brain fog at 30% (95% CI 28-32) and cognitive impairment at 25% (23-27), higher in women, community-managed and unvaccinated patients, and with longer follow-up.
reason: Measures symptom prevalence in long COVID, not domain-specific neuropsychological deficits in ME/CFS; no atlas finding covers long COVID cognitive-symptom prevalence.
